uncertainty_flags: No multi-seed averages or standard deviations for accuracy and timing; sampling and REINFORCE introduce stochasticity.
Timing measurement lacks hardware and batching details and separates no-component-level profiling.
REINFORCE gradient variance and convergence diagnostics absent; only end-result performance reported.
Sparse final reward (±1) may produce high-variance or dataset-specific policies; no ablations with denser rewards shown.
No aggregate statistics of jump behavior (distributions of jump lengths, early stopping rates) to rule out degenerate strategies.
alternative_interpretations: Accuracy gains on CBT might stem from truncation/padding/preprocessing that favors early stopping combined with dataset-specific structure rather than generalized learned skipping.

Reported wall-clock speedups could be partly due to differences in batch sizes or implementation optimizations rather than purely algorithmic token savings; smaller models/tasks show less speedup indicating implementation overhead matters.
Positive synthetic results reflect a task with clear, easily discoverable skip signal—real-world gains may be smaller or require careful task-specific tuning.
transparency_notes: Manuscript includes code base note (TensorFlow) but does not give link; providing code and scripts to reproduce timing/hyperparameter experiments would materially improve reproducibility.
Key hyperparameters are reported (R,K,N, Adam lr, dropout), but missing are training run counts, random seeds, exact hardware, and loss weighting details for joint objective.

Related-work discussion situates contribution among attention, adaptive computation, and RL-based controllers; however empirical comparisons to alternative adaptive methods (e.g., Graves 2016) are not provided.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The idea of hard discrete jumps in text with REINFORCE is relatively uncommon compared to soft attention or differentiable adaptive computation; sparse precedent suggests potential novelty. However, novelty does not by itself establish empirical robustness—training stability, variance, and reproducibility must be demonstrated.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the task exhibits local, strong skip signals (as in synthetic data) or queries that localize relevant context (CBT), then a learned jump policy can reliably skip and improve speed/accuracy.

If denser or shaped rewards (e.g., intermediate rewards for hitting informative segments) or improved variance reduction (actor-critic) are employed, training could become more stable and generalizable.
If deployment uses greedy inference or ensembles over sampled jumps to reduce variance, observed test-time performance may become more predictable and practically useful.
If hardware/batching and implementation overheads are optimized (e.g., vectorized skipping, reduced softmax overhead), wall-clock speedups will be more robust across setups.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines known components (LSTM, REINFORCE baseline) in a new operational configuration (discrete jumping controller for text skipping) with practical engineering results across diverse datasets. Similar in spirit to hard-attention and adaptive computation but distinct in action-space and target of inference-speed optimization.
evidence: Related Work cites attention-based RL (Mnih et al.), hard attention for rationales (Lei et al.), and adaptive computation (Graves); LSTM-Jump occupies an intermediate, application-focused niche.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of novelty depends on proximity to concurrent works (Shen et al., Choi et al.) and how much the joint REINFORCE formulation differs in practice; manuscript does not fully map differences quantitatively.

novelty_lenses.verdict: limited disruptive potential until robustness is shown
novelty_lenses.rationale: If reliably generalizable, the approach could alter how long-text NLP models are deployed by allowing hard skipping to reduce inference cost. But current evidence is task-limited and lacks robustness diagnostics, constraining disruptive claims.
evidence: Large synthetic and CBT speedups are promising, but lack of profiling, variance analysis, and multi-seed reproducibility reduces confidence in general deployment impact.
uncertainty_flags: Significant engineering and methodology work (profiling, training-stability improvements, reproducibility) needed before asserting broad disruptive potential.

confidence_interval.rationale: I place moderate confidence that the core idea is feasible and that the empirical numbers are accurate for the reported setups (supported by many per-task results). However, due to missing variance reporting, under-specified timing methodology, and lack of RL stability diagnostics, confidence in the method's robustness and generalization to other datasets/hardware is substantially lower. The interval reflects strong evidence for feasibility but substantial uncertainty about generality and reproducibility.

consensus_findings: The manuscript defines a clear, implementable architecture (LSTM-Jump) that augments an LSTM with discrete jump decisions parameterized by (R, K, N) and describes a joint training objective combining supervised loss for the reader and REINFORCE (with a learned linear baseline) for the jump policy.

Authors provide a reasonably broad empirical sweep: synthetic sanity checks plus multiple real datasets (sentiment, news, character-level, and sentence-level QA) showing reductions in 'avg tokens read' and reported wall-clock test-time improvements alongside comparable or sometimes improved test accuracy.
The idea of hard discrete skipping controlled by a learned policy is methodologically plausible and operationally distinct from soft-attention or differentiable adaptive-computation approaches.

Key methodological and reporting gaps are present across reviewers: missing multi-seed statistics, absent timing/environmental/profiling details, lack of training/variance diagnostics for REINFORCE, no ablation of reward/baseline choices, and no aggregate diagnostics of learned jump behavior to rule out degenerate policies.
disagreements: Novelty characterization: some reviewers view the contribution as an incremental but meaningful engineering combination of known ideas (hard attention + RL + adaptive computation) while others treat the discrete-jump instantiation as a more novel, promising conceptual frame. Both perspectives agree on relevance but differ on the level of novelty claim.

Sufficiency of REINFORCE as presented: some reviewers accept that REINFORCE+linear baseline is an adequate initial demonstration (given empirical successes), whereas others judge the lack of variance/convergence diagnostics and alternative-RL ablations as preventing the claim that REINFORCE is broadly 'effective' in this setting.

Interpretation of reported speedups: reviewers agree speedups are reported but disagree on how much those numbers reflect algorithmic savings versus implementation/hardware/batching artifacts—some emphasize likely implementation dependence more strongly than others.

Extent to which observed accuracy gains imply meaningful selective reading: some reviewers interpret CBT/synthetic gains as evidence that skipping helps generalization, while others caution that gains could alternatively reflect implicit regularization, dataset artifacts, or preprocessing choices.
uncertainty_hotspots: Training stability and gradient variance for the REINFORCE component: no reported training curves, gradient-variance estimates, number of policy samples S per update, or experiments with alternative variance-reduction (actor-critic, richer baselines, advantage normalization).

Test-time inference policy and variability: sampling is used at inference but no comparison to deterministic (greedy) argmax or multi-run variance estimates are provided; test-time stochasticity may affect reproducibility and deployment suitability.

Timing and profiling methodology: hardware (GPU/CPU model), batching strategy during timed runs, number of timing repeats, warm-up runs, and a micro-profile separating jump-control overhead (softmax/sampling) from recurrent-step computation are missing.

Reward design and credit assignment: using a single final reward (+1/−1) is sparse and may permit degenerate strategies; no ablation of reward shaping, per-step penalties, or intermediate rewards is shown.

Behavioral diagnostics of learned policies: no aggregate statistics (histograms of jump lengths, stop-time distributions, per-example read fractions) to detect trivial or dataset-specific policies (e.g., always stop early).
Reproducibility details: missing code repository link, random seeds used, exact REINFORCE hyperparameters (S, baseline init), and full training schedules impede replication.
model_diversity_effects: Role emphasis effects: structure_analyst prioritized logical chain and breakpoints (highlighting the dependence of empirical claims on stability/timing evidence); methodology_auditor prioritized reproducibility protocols and variance diagnostics; novelty_assessors split on whether the contribution is incremental versus conceptually novel, affecting how strongly they judged the paper's impact; claim_verifier focused on evidence sufficiency and conservative interpretation of empirical numbers.

Consequent evaluation differences: reviewers with a reproducibility lens flagged missing experiment-reporting items as critical (timing, multi-seed runs, training curves), while novelty-focused reviewers were more willing to treat sparse prior art as an innovation signal but still requested robustness checks. These complementary perspectives together indicate that the paper shows a promising idea but requires stronger empirical and reporting rigor to support broader claims.

Role-specific effect on uncertainty: reviewers emphasizing implementation/engineering (novelty_assessor_incremental) were more tolerant of single-run results as proof-of-concept; reviewers emphasizing methodological validity demanded ablations and multiple-seed statistics, raising epistemic caution. This diversity increases confidence that the idea is workable but lowers confidence about its robustness and generalizability.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as a promising methodological/engineering contribution that demonstrates feasibility but requires targeted additional evidence before its empirical claims can be generalized. Request the authors to (1) provide reproducibility artifacts (public code, exact configs and seeds), (2) report multi-seed means and standard deviations for key accuracy and timing numbers and perform simple statistical tests for reported gains, (3) fully specify the timing protocol (hardware, device placement, batch sizes, warm-ups) and include per-component profiling separating jump overhead from recurrent computation, (4) add training diagnostics (training curves for supervised loss and policy reward, estimates of gradient variance or policy entropy over time), (5) include ablations of RL design choices (baseline variants, number of policy samples S, reward shaping or intermediate rewards, and at least one alternative such as a simple actor-critic or continuous relaxation on a representative task), and (6) report aggregate behavioral diagnostics of the jump policy (histograms of jump lengths, stop-time rates, per-class behavior) and compare sampling vs greedy inference at test time. Keep the editor's decision central: these items are necessary for assessing the generality and robustness of the reported speed/accuracy trade-offs.
meta_review.author_guidance: To substantiate and clarify the paper's empirical claims, provide the following: (1) Release code and exact experiment scripts (training and timing) with noted random seeds. (2) For representative configurations (synthetic long sequence, IMDB, CBT), run and report results over multiple random seeds (recommended ≥5) including mean and standard deviation for accuracy, avg tokens read, and wall-clock time; include statistical tests for key comparisons. (3) Describe the timing protocol in detail: hardware model(s), whether GPU/CPU used, batch sizes during timed runs, number of repeats, and whether embedding loading/warm-up is included; add micro-profiling that reports time (or FLOP proxies) spent on RNN steps versus jump softmax and sampling to attribute speedups. (4) Provide training diagnostics: learning curves for supervised loss, policy reward, and policy entropy over epochs; report number of training steps to convergence. (5) Ablate RL components: vary baseline type (constant, linear, small MLP), report number of Monte Carlo samples S used for gradient estimates, test alternative variance-reduction / RL methods (simple actor-critic or advantage normalization) on one or two tasks, and test reward shaping (intermediate rewards or small per-token read penalty). (6) Characterize learned policies: histograms of jump lengths, distribution of stop times, per-example read fraction, and qualitative examples; check for degenerate policies (e.g., always stop early) and robustness under small input perturbations. (7) Compare sampling vs greedy inference at test time (and optionally ensemble sampling) and report variance induced by sampling. (8) Where possible, run a small head-to-head to a representative adaptive-computation baseline (e.g., ACT or another cited method) on a single task to contextualize gains. Prioritize including the above in a revised manuscript or supplementary material to enable confident interpretation and reproducibility.
transparency_report: Missing or under-specified items flagged by reviewers: no public repository link for the exact implementation; no random-seed listing or multi-seed results; REINFORCE-specific hyperparameters missing (number of policy samples S per gradient update, any entropy regularization, baseline initialization).

Timing/profiling omissions: hardware (GPU/CPU type), batch sizes used for timed evaluations, number of timing runs and warm-up policy, and micro-profiling separating jump softmax/sampling overhead from recurrent-step time are not reported.

Training diagnostics absent: no training curves for supervised loss or policy reward, no reporting of policy entropy or gradient variance, and no details on curriculum schedule (when used) such as lengths per stage or epochs per stage.
Behavioral diagnostics missing: no aggregate distributions of jump lengths, stop-time histograms, per-example tokens-read distributions, or identification of possible degenerate/shortcut strategies.
Comparative and ablation omissions: no comparisons of sampling vs greedy inference, no ablation of baseline capacity or alternate RL methods, no exploration of reward shaping or intermediate rewards.

Some per-task choices reported (embedding fixed vs trainable, hidden sizes) but inconsistent preprocessing and augmentation across tasks (e.g., segment sampling for Rotten Tomatoes) may confound attribution; these choices should be fully enumerated and matched in controlled comparisons.
epistemic_limits: Current reviews and shared analysis cannot establish (a) reproducibility: single-run numbers and missing code/hardware/seeds prevent independent replication; (b) robustness of REINFORCE training: absence of gradient-variance and convergence diagnostics leaves uncertainty about stability across seeds and tasks; (c) generalization to arbitrary long/untruncated documents and different hardware: timing/profiling gaps mean observed speedups may be implementation- or hardware-specific; (d) causal attribution of accuracy gains: without ablations the improvements may derive from implicit regularization, curriculum, or preprocessing rather than the jump mechanism itself; (e) extent of test-time variability induced by sampling: without multi-run sampling statistics, deployment suitability and worst-case behaviors cannot be assessed. These are empirical limits (not theoretical invalidations): the paper plausibly demonstrates feasibility in the reported setups, but broader claims about generality, stability, and deployment readiness require the additional evidence and diagnostics recommended above.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces LSTM-Jump: an LSTM augmented with a learned discrete jump controller (parameters R, K, N) that samples jump lengths to skip parts of the input. The controller is trained with policy-gradient (REINFORCE) using a single final reward (+1/−1) and a learned linear baseline; LSTM weights are trained with supervised cross-entropy in a joint objective. Experiments on a synthetic task and four real datasets (sentiment, news, character-level, and sentence-level QA) report large reductions in average tokens read and wall-clock inference time (very large on synthetic; up to ~6x on CBT) while maintaining or sometimes improving accuracy compared to a vanilla LSTM. Reviewers agree the idea is implementable and promising but identified important methodological and reporting gaps (multi-seed statistics, timing/profiling details, REINFORCE variance diagnostics, policy-behavior analyses, and ablations of RL design), which limit confidence in generality and reproducibility.
strengths: Clear, implementable architecture with concise operational specification (R, K, N), stopping rules, and mapping from hidden state to discrete jump softmax.
Principled training formulation combining supervised loss for the reader and REINFORCE with a learned baseline for the discrete jump controller, with explicit derivations.

Diverse empirical evaluation: synthetic sanity check plus multiple real datasets across token granularities (character/word/sentence) demonstrating feasibility and measurable speed/accuracy trade-offs.
Practical reporting of both algorithmic proxies (avg tokens read) and wall-clock test-time measurements, showing where the method can yield substantial inference savings.
limitations: Timing and profiling under-specified: hardware (CPU/GPU models), batching strategy for timed runs, number of repeats/warm-ups, and micro-profiling (time spent in recurrent steps vs jump softmax/sampling) are not reported, so wall-clock speedups may be implementation- or hardware-dependent.

Lack of multi-seed statistics and significance testing: reported accuracies and timing are single-run numbers without means/std devs, so small reported gains may be within run-to-run variation (especially since inference uses stochastic sampling).

Insufficient diagnostics for REINFORCE training: no training curves (reward/entropy/supervised loss), no gradient-variance estimates, and no ablation of baseline capacity or alternative variance-reduction methods; this leaves training stability and general applicability uncertain.

Sparse episodic reward and potential for degenerate policies: using only a final +1/−1 reward risks high variance and permits trivial strategies (e.g., immediate stop) that could exploit dataset or preprocessing artifacts; the manuscript lacks aggregate behavioral analyses (jump-length histograms, stop-time distributions) to rule this out.

Inconsistent per-task preprocessing/embedding choices: embedding treatments (fixed vs trainable), truncation/augmentation and model capacities vary by dataset and could confound attribution of accuracy or convergence differences to the jump mechanism alone.
open_questions: Please provide detailed timing protocol and profiling: on which hardware were timed runs performed (GPU/CPU model), what batch sizes and device placements were used at test time, how many timing runs/warm-ups were averaged, and micro-benchmarks separating time spent on recurrent steps vs jump softmax and sampling?

Provide variability estimates: for key configurations (representative synthetic long sequence, IMDB, CBT) run ≥5 seeds and report mean±std for accuracy, avg tokens read, and wall-clock time; are the reported improvements statistically significant under these repeats?

Characterize learned policies: supply histograms of sampled jump lengths, distributions of stopping times, average number of jumps per example, and example trajectories across seeds; do any degenerate policies (e.g., always stop immediately) arise?

Provide training diagnostics and RL ablations: training curves for supervised loss, policy reward, and policy entropy; number of Monte Carlo samples S used per policy gradient update; and ablations comparing linear baseline to alternatives (constant baseline, small MLP) and at least one alternative RL/variance-reduction method (actor-critic or advantage normalization).

Compare inference modes: how do sampling (used in experiments) and greedy (argmax) decoding compare in accuracy and runtime variance at test time? If sampling stabilizes accuracy as an implicit ensemble, report recommended deployment practice.

Clarify curriculum and optimization details: where curriculum was used, provide explicit schedule (sequence lengths per stage, epochs per stage, stopping thresholds) and report whether joint vs staged training (pretrain reader then policy, alternate updates) was tried and how it affects convergence.
consensus_snapshot: Architecture and joint REINFORCE-based training are clearly specified and implementable; empirical results show the idea can work in the reported setups.

Reported reductions in avg tokens read and wall-clock inference time along with comparable or improved accuracy are promising and consistent across multiple tasks, but the magnitude of wall-clock speedups may depend on implementation/hardware.

Methodological/reporting gaps are material and shared across reviewers: missing multi-seed statistics, missing timing/profiling details, missing RL-variance diagnostics, lack of policy-behavior analyses, and insufficient ablations of RL design and reward shaping.
disagreement_snapshot: Novelty: some reviewers regard the contribution as an incremental engineering combination of existing ideas (hard attention + adaptive computation + REINFORCE), while others see the discrete jump instantiation for text as a more novel operational frame. Both views accept practical relevance but disagree on novelty magnitude.

Sufficiency of REINFORCE: a subset of reviewers consider REINFORCE+linear baseline adequate as a proof-of-concept given empirical success; others require explicit variance and stability diagnostics and alternate-RL ablations before endorsing the claim that policy-gradient is broadly effective here.

Interpretation of small accuracy differences: some reviewers accept modest accuracy changes as meaningful (especially on CBT/synthetic), while others treat small deltas (e.g., 0.793 vs 0.791) as likely within noise absent statistical tests.
uncertainty_snapshot: High uncertainty about generalizability to other hardware and production settings due to missing profiling and timing protocol details.
Substantial uncertainty about reproducibility and run-to-run variability because experiments lack multi-seed reporting and inference is stochastic.
Moderate to high uncertainty about training stability and whether REINFORCE will scale to broader tasks without additional variance-reduction or reward shaping, since diagnostics are not reported.

Uncertainty whether observed accuracy gains are due to meaningful selective reading or indirect effects (implicit regularization, dataset-specific preprocessing) because ablations and policy behavior diagnostics are absent.

transparency_notes: Key reproducibility and transparency gaps identified: no public repository link for the exact implementation and experiment scripts; missing random-seed listings and absent multi-seed result reporting; REINFORCE-specific hyperparameters not fully enumerated (number of policy samples S per update, entropy regularization, baseline initialization); timing/profiling protocol underspecified (hardware, batch sizes, number of timing runs/warm-ups); curriculum schedules and per-stage details not provided; no aggregate diagnostics of jump behavior (histograms of jump lengths, stop-time rates) or training diagnostics (reward, loss, entropy curves). Providing these artifacts and numeric diagnostics (means/stds) would materially improve reproducibility and interpretability.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as a promising proof-of-concept that requires targeted additional evidence before claims of broad effectiveness can be assessed. If a revision is invited, require the authors to (a) release code and exact training/evaluation scripts with seeds; (b) report multi-seed (recommended ≥5) mean±std for key accuracy and timing numbers and perform simple statistical tests for main comparisons; (c) fully document timing protocol and include micro-profiling (recurrent-step vs jump softmax/sampling overhead); (d) provide training diagnostics (learning curves for supervised loss and policy reward, policy entropy, and number of training iterations to convergence); (e) perform ablations of RL design (baseline variants, number of policy samples S, at least one alternative such as actor-critic or advantage normalization, and reward-shaping experiments); and (f) include policy-behavior analyses (jump-length and stop-time histograms, sample trajectories) and compare sampling vs greedy inference at test time. These items are necessary for assessing generality, stability, and deployment readiness; absence of them leaves critical uncertainties.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical and methodological claims, provide the following in a revision or supplementary material: (1) Public code repository with training and evaluation scripts and configuration files (including random seeds). (2) For representative settings (one long synthetic configuration, one IMDB setting, one CBT setting) run ≥5 independent seeds and report mean±std for accuracy, avg tokens read, and wall-clock time; include simple statistical tests for key comparisons. (3) Exhaustive timing protocol: hardware (GPU/CPU models), batch sizes, device placement, number of timing runs and warm-ups, and micro-profile splitting time spent on recurrent steps, embedding lookup, jump softmax and sampling, and other overheads. (4) Training diagnostics: curves for supervised loss, expected reward, policy entropy; estimates of gradient variance or batch-level reward variance; the number of policy-gradient samples S used per update. (5) RL ablations: linear vs richer baselines (e.g., small MLP), varying S, alternative variance-reduction techniques (actor-critic/advantage), and experiments with reward shaping (intermediate rewards, per-token penalties). (6) Behavioral analyses of learned policies: histograms of jump lengths and stopping times, fraction of trivial/degenerate strategies, per-class behavior, and robustness to small input perturbations. (7) Compare inference modes: sampling vs greedy argmax vs ensembles of samples and report the variance introduced by sampling. (8) Where feasible add a head-to-head comparison to a representative adaptive-computation baseline (e.g., ACT) on one dataset to contextualize trade-offs. Prioritize multi-seed reporting and timing/profiling as these most strongly affect the manuscript's main claims.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper presents LSTM-Jump, an LSTM augmented with a discrete jump controller trained with REINFORCE (learned linear baseline). The joint training objective and stopping rules are clearly specified. Empirical evaluation on synthetic and four real datasets across different token granularities shows substantial reductions in average tokens read and wall-clock inference time while maintaining or sometimes improving accuracy versus a vanilla LSTM.

Strengths:
- Implementable architecture and clear operational details (R, K, N, stopping criteria). 
- Principled joint training formulation integrating supervised loss and REINFORCE with a learned baseline. 
- Broad empirical sweep across synthetic and multiple real tasks at character/word/sentence granularities. 
- Reporting of both avg tokens read and wall-clock time, enabling practical efficiency claims.

Limitations:
- Timing/profiling details missing: hardware, batch sizes, warm-ups, repeats, and micro-benchmarks separating jump overhead from recurrent computation are not provided; wall-clock speedups may be implementation-dependent.
- No multi-seed or statistical reporting: accuracy/time are single-run numbers without mean±std or significance tests; sampling at inference introduces stochasticity that can produce run-to-run variation.
- REINFORCE diagnostics absent: no training curves, gradient-variance estimates, or ablations on baseline capacity or alternative variance-reduction methods; training stability across seeds/tasks is uncertain.
- Sparse final reward permits possible degenerate policies: the manuscript lacks aggregate behavioral diagnostics (jump-length histograms, stop-time distributions) to confirm policies are meaningful rather than trivial shortcuts.
- Per-task preprocessing/embedding differences may confound attributions: embedding update choices, truncation/augmentation, and differing model capacities are not controlled across comparisons.

Open Questions:
- What exact timing protocol and profiling data can the authors provide (hardware, batch sizes, number of timing runs/warm-ups, per-component times)?
- Can the authors present multi-seed results (recommended ≥5 runs) with mean±std for accuracy, avg tokens read, and wall-clock time for representative configurations to assess variability and statistical significance?
- What are the distributions of learned jump lengths and stopping times across datasets and seeds? Do degenerate strategies occur? Please provide histograms and example trajectories.
- What RL hyperparameters were used exactly (number of policy samples S per gradient update, any entropy regularization, baseline initialization)? Can the authors ablate baseline types and compare at least one alternative variance-reduction method (actor-critic or advantage normalization)?
- How does sampling at inference compare to greedy argmax decoding in accuracy and runtime variance? What inference mode do the authors recommend for deployment?
- Where curriculum was required (synthetic), please provide explicit schedule and experiments comparing joint vs staged training to clarify optimization practices.

Transparency:
Critical reproducibility gaps: no public repository link with exact code/scripts and seeds; missing REINFORCE hyperparameters (S, baseline init), missing timing/profiling protocol, absent training curves and gradient-variance diagnostics, missing policy-behavior aggregates, and inconsistent per-task preprocessing/embedding choices that should be enumerated and controlled in ablations. Including these materials and diagnostics would substantially improve reproducibility and interpretability.

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects uncertainty due to missing multi-seed statistics, timing/profiling details, and RL stability diagnostics which materially affect reproducibility and generalization. Upper bound reflects that the idea is well-specified, implemented, and demonstrated across multiple datasets in the manuscript, providing credible feasibility evidence for the reported setups.

We would like to be able to capture regularities in such structures, or to model similarities between such structures. In many cases, this means encoding the structure as a ﬁxed width vector, which we can then pass on to another statistical learner for further processing. While convolutional and pooling architectures allow us to encode arbitrary large items as ﬁxed size vectors capturing their most salient features, they do so by sacriﬁcing most of the structural information. Recurrent (Section 10) and recursive (Section 12) architectures, on the other hand, allow us to work with sequences and trees while preserving a lot of the structural information. Recurrent networks (Elman, 1990) are designed to model sequences, while recursive networks (Goller & K¨ uchler, 1996) are generalizations of recurrent networks that can handle trees. We will also discuss an extension of recurrent networks that allow them to model stacks (Dyer, Ballesteros, Ling, Matthews, & Smith, 2015; Watanabe & Sumita, 2015). Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

The rapid adoption of RNNs in NLP systems in recent years, in particular of RNNs with gating mecha- nisms such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) or gated recur- rent units (GRU) (Cho et al., 2014), has led to sig- niﬁcant gains in language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sundermeyer et al., 2012), parsing (Vinyals et al., 2015; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016; Dyer et al., 2016), machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and other tasks. The effectiveness of RNNs1 is attributed to their ability to capture statistical contingencies that may span an arbitrary number of words. The wordFrance, for example, is more likely to occur somewhere in a sentence that begins with Paris than in a sentence that begins with Penguins. The fact that an arbitrary number of words can intervene between the mutually predictive words implies that they cannot be captured by models with a ﬁxed window such asn-gram mod- els, but can in principle be captured by RNNs, which do not have an architecturally ﬁxed limit on depen- dency length.

Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

The rapid adoption of RNNs in NLP systems in recent years, in particular of RNNs with gating mecha- nisms such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) or gated recur- rent units (GRU) (Cho et al., 2014), has led to sig- niﬁcant gains in language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sundermeyer et al., 2012), parsing (Vinyals et al., 2015; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016; Dyer et al., 2016), machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and other tasks. The effectiveness of RNNs1 is attributed to their ability to capture statistical contingencies that may span an arbitrary number of words. The wordFrance, for example, is more likely to occur somewhere in a sentence that begins with Paris than in a sentence that begins with Penguins. The fact that an arbitrary number of words can intervene between the mutually predictive words implies that they cannot be captured by models with a ﬁxed window such asn-gram mod- els, but can in principle be captured by RNNs, which do not have an architecturally ﬁxed limit on depen- dency length.

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
